newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle astronauts complete second spacewalk.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle astronauts complete second spacewalk.

text.p: Shuttle astronauts installed a new targeting device in the Hubble Space Telescope on Saturday and reported parts of the observatory's protective skin were tattered and torn.
Discovery astronauts Greg Harbaugh and Joe Tanner carefully removed an ageing guidance sensor and replaced it with a new device fitted with special optics to correct for Hubble's misshapen mirror.

"Ever so gently," cautioned Harbaugh as Tanner gingerly manoeuvred the 492-pound (223 kg) sensor, about the size of a baby grand piano. "I think it's in there, yes sir!" Harbaugh said as the delicate instrument slid into place.
Tanner worked perched on the end of the shuttle's 50-foot (15-metre) robot arm, while Harbaugh assisted, tethered to the telescope like a mountain climber.

David Leckrone, Hubble senior project scientist, compared the accuracy of the new targeting device to being able to hit a golf ball in Washington, D.C., and score a hole-in-one in Denver, Colorado. "They're very precise, very complex optical instruments and we're absolutely dependent on them to do science," he said.

The $8 million device would determine the position of stars about 10 times more precisely than ground-based telescopes. Astronomers also hoped to use it to detect tiny wobbles in the motion of nearby stars that might indicate the presence of an orbiting planet.

The astronauts then tackled the replacement of a broken tape recorder and a quick wiring job for the new guidance sensor before returning the shuttle's airlock. The spacewalk lasted just over seven hours, longer than expected, partly because mission control ordered additional inspections of Hubble's tattered and tarnished exterior.
The astronauts reported that the harsh environment of space had taken its toll. Paint was discoloured and in places silvery insulation foil was torn and peeling away from Hubble's skin.

"In several places it's cracked. It's just gotten old, it looks like," Harbaugh radioed mission control. Some of the tears were 18 inches (46 cm) long, he said. "They're not just tiny little spider cracks."

The wear and tear was not present when astronauts first visited the telescope in 1993 to fix its blurred vision. "We did not see anything like this," veteran astronaut Story Musgrave, who led the spacewalks on that mission, said.

Mission managers formed a team of engineers to consider ways of repairing the foil, the first of up to 20 layers of material that protect the telescope from harsh temperature changes. "The specific concern is if that starts breaking off then it could contaminate the optics and then degrade the capabilities of the telescope," said astronaut Jerry Ross at mission control.

NASA officials thought it unlikely the astronauts could do much about the damage during the current mission but repairs might be possible when the shuttle next visits the telescope in 1999. "As bad as it looked, we probably can survive until '99," Kenneth Ledbetter said at NASA headquarters.

The astronauts also spotted numerous space debris hits on the telescope's 40-foot (12-metre)-long electricity-generating solar panels. "That's like somebody shot a small calibre bullet right through it," Tanner said as he videotaped one hole in the solar cells.

One of the astronauts' final tasks of the day was to gently ease Hubble two miles (3.2 km) higher with a 20-minute series of bursts from the shuttle's precision manoeuvring jets. Later in the day the shuttle's orbit was boosted a further half-mile (0.8km) as a precaution to avoid a passing chunk of space debris.
NASA wants to boost the telescope's altitude by about five miles (8 km) to prolong its lifetime. Further jet firings are planned over the next two days.
